newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says he "badly out of shape" for debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says he "badly out of shape" for debate.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday jokingly played down his prospects in Sunday's debate with Republican rival Bob Dole, and said he wants the televised clash to be "genuinely informative" for the voters.

"I'm badly out of shape on this, but I'm trying to get better," a smiling, relaxed Clinton told reporters as he emerged from a lakeside hotel serving as his pre-debate headquarters to soak up a bit of the glorious autumn weather at the Chautauqua Institution, a quiet Victorian-era resort in western New York State.

Turning to former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell, who is impersonating Dole in dress rehearsals for the Hartford, Conn. debate on Sunday night, Clinton said: "Tell the truth, George. You beat me like a drum. You kicked me all over the place last night."
Buttressing the president's effort to lower expectations, Mitchell said he probably debated Dole more than anyone else when they were in the Senate together "and I know just how effective he is."
"Senator Dole is a highly skilled debater, and I think he's going to be tough in this debate coming up on Sunday. But the president, I think, will do all right," he said.
Dole, in Bal Harbour, Florida, was also playing the traditional pre-debate game of downplaying his chances as his advisers emphasised Clinton's rhetorical skills.
Clinton, casually dressed in brown slacks and a brown sweater with necktie, said campaign debates "are tough" because perceptions count as much as answering hard questions.
"The most important thing is to remember that this debate is as much about the American people and their lives and their future as it is about Senator Dole and me," he said.

"My objectives are fairly straightforward and basically quite simple: I want to make sure that the voters know what the record is, they know what the contrasts are between Senator Dole and me, and most important of all, that they know what I intend to do for the next four years."

"I think my goal here is to make sure that the people actually get something out of this debate other than just sort of an exercise in who does a better job in outwitting someone else. I think it ought to be something that's genuinely informative, and I'm going to try to make it that way," Clinton said.

He did not give a direct reply when asked how he would respond to a likely question about whether he would use his pardon power to spring friends and associates convicted of Whitewater-related offences from jail.

"There aren't any under consideration, and I haven't given any thought to giving any. That's not the issue ... I think that nobody should be singled out for special treatment one way or the other, including discrimination against them or discrimination for them," he said.

Political experts said Clinton, who leads Dole in national opinion polls by 10 to 18 percentage points less than five weeks before the Nov. 5 election, had an obvious strategy for the debate: hammer the theme that Americans are better off now than they were four years ago and avoid gaffes like those made by Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter and George Bush.

Ford said at the height of the Cold War that Poland was not dominated by the Soviet Union; Carter said he had discussed nuclear strategy with his young daughter Amy; and Bush glanced at his wristwatch, creating the impression that he was indifferent to the concerns of ordinary people.

As Clinton prepared for his match up with Dole, his aides chortled about a new sign of the Republican's political troubles -- a new set of ads for Republican congressional candidates that omit any mention of Dole.

Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart, a veteran of disasterous Democratic presidential campaigns against Republican Ronald Reagan, said: "It's what we used to call back in the 1980s 'lifeboat day.'"
